Amanda Scarpone Poland LD 1120
Amanda Scarpone Poland, Maine April 15, 2025
To Members of the Judiciary Committee:
Thank you for the opportunity to address the Committee. My name is Amanda Scarpone, I am a resident of Poland, Maine, and I am a public health professional who works in the non-profit and philanthropy field. I am also a member of the Maine Public Health Association.
I am writing to you today in support of LD 1120, An Act to Promote the Secure Storage of Firearms. As a public health professional, I believe in the need for gun safety measures to protect us all. Maine has a strong culture of responsible gun ownership, but this does not free us from the risk and devastation of gun violence. This was unfortunately made clear in the tragic mass shooting in Lewiston, ME--a tragedy that has irrevocably altered many lives and our community as a whole.
There are ways that we can decrease the risk of gun violence in Maine, as well as decrease gun deaths by suicide. A clear method is through safe storage, which is promoted by LD 1120. Safe storage laws allow responsible gun owners to securely keep their firearms, while keeping firearms out of the hands of those who could intentionally or unintentionally do harm. Currently, more than half of gun owners do not securely store their firearms. When guns are not safely stored, it increases access to death by suicide using a firearm, accidental shootings in the home, and firearm theft and illicit activity. Maine has the 38th highest gun death rate in the US, and gun deaths in Maine have increased 50% from 2014-2023, and death by gun suicide has increased 34%. We can do more improve those grim statistics. We can do more to protect Mainers by preventing death by gun suicide, accidental gun deaths, as well as preventing firearm theft. LD 1120 is a clear policy to do just that.
Thank you for the opportunity to share my perspective with the Committee. I urge you to vote "Ought to Pass" on LD 1120.
Thank you, Amanda Scarpone

TESTIMONY OF THE MAINE MEDICAL ASSOCIATION AND
THE MAINE OSTEOPATHIC ASSOCIATION

In Support Of

LD 1104 - An Act to Limit the Liability of Persons Who Provide Firearm Hold Agreements; and LD 1174 - An Act to Allow Gun Shops to Hold Firearms for Veterans of the United States Armed Forces and First Responders; LD 1120 - An Act to Promote the Secure Storage of Firearms; and LD 1299
An Act to Prohibit the Unsecured Storage of Handguns in Motor Vehicles  Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary Room 438, State House, Augusta, Maine Wednesday, April 16, 2025

Good Afternoon, Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary. My name is Anne Sedlack, and I am the Director of Advocacy at the Maine Medical Association. I am submitting this testimony in Support of LD 1104 - An Act to Limit the Liability of Persons Who Provide Firearm Hold Agreements, LD 1174 - An Act to Allow Gun Shops to Hold Firearms for Veterans of the United States Armed Forces and First Responders, LD 1120 An Act to Promote the Secure Storage of Firearms, and LD 1299 An Act to Prohibit the Unsecured Storage of Handguns in Motor Vehicles on behalf of the Maine Medical Association and Maine Osteopathic Association.

The Maine Medical Association (MMA) is a professional organization representing more than 4,000 physicians, residents, and medical students in Maine. MMA's mission is to support Maine physicians, advance the quality of medicine in Maine, and promote the health of all Maine people. The Maine Osteopathic Association (MOA) is a professional organization representing more than 1,200 osteopathic physicians, residents, and medical students in Maine whose mission is to serve the Osteopathic profession of the State of Maine through a coordinated effort of professional education, advocacy, and member services in order to ensure the availability of quality osteopathic health care to the people of this State.

We have joined together to advocate with one voice. We have all determined that it is important to testify in support of LD 1104, LD 1174, LD 1120, and LD 1299.

MMA and MOA have chosen gun safety reform as a priority issue for our Associations because we cannot continue to ignore one of America's most serious public health crises. Deaths by firearms have increased significantly in the last few years, including homicide, suicide, and accidents. We, the physician caregivers for more than a million Mainers, stand up to end this and advocate through the protection of existing state law and the passage of sensible firearm safety laws in Maine. Maine's physicians are dedicated to our communities' health and well-being. We take our role in advancing public health measures seriously. We have no choice because we are on the front lines of caring for patients affected by gun-related injuries every day.

LD 1174 and LD 1104 provide a compassionate, voluntary solution to a legitimate public health crisis, the alarmingly high rates of firearm suicides among both veterans and first responders. As doctors, we regularly interact with patients in the midst of mental health crises, and we know better than almost anyone how lethal access to firearms can be in a moment of mental crisis. The practice of temporarily removing firearms from individuals in crisis, especially with their consent in a respectful manner, is a powerful tool to prevent suicides.
LD 1174 would allow licensed gun shops to enter into formal "firearm hold agreements" with veterans and first responders who voluntarily wish to store their firearms for safekeeping. By codifying this option and protecting participating gun shops from liability when acting in good faith, the bill creates a clear, safe pathway for individuals to reduce immediate risk without permanently relinquishing their firearms. LD 1104 further complements LD 1174 by offering commonsense liability protections to those who voluntarily agree to hold firearms under a firearm hold agreement. Together, these two bills remove key obstacles to safe firearm storage, an essential part of preventing suicide, by giving people the confidence and clarity they need to step in and help. Encouraging temporary safekeeping during times of crisis can save lives and strengthen a culture of care and responsibility within our communities.
We also support LD 1120 and LD 1299. Maine currently has no law requiring the secure storage of firearms, aside from a law penalizing those who allow young children to access firearms without parental permission, but this law is not enough. These two bills offer common-sense, lifesaving policies that address the significant public health concern of unsecured firearms in homes and vehicles.
LD 1120 lays out rules to help keep guns out of the hands of kids and people who shouldn't have them, something that can go a long way in preventing accidental shootings, suicides, and domestic violence. It also makes sure gun dealers give buyers clear warnings about the risks that come with owning a firearm. LD 1299 tackles the growing problem of handguns being stolen from unattended vehicles, which are often later used in crimes. In fact, one study has found that firearms that are stolen are nine times more likely to be used in a crime than guns purchased legally.1 LD 1129 would help address this problem by requiring that guns be locked up and kept out of sight while being stored in a vehicle. By doing this, the bill aims to cut down on gun theft and help keep our communities safer.
Thank you for considering the thoughts of Maine's physicians and public health community. We hope you will support these bills.
Best,
Anne Sedlack Director of Advocacy Maine Medical Association Email: asedlack@mainephysicians.org

Testimony in support of LD 1120, An Act to Promote the Secure Storage of Firearms, and LD 1299, An Act to Prohibit the Unsecured Storage of Handguns in Motor Vehicles April 16, 2025
Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Honorable Members of the Judiciary Committee, my name is Art Blank and I live in Bar Harbor and am submitting this testimony representing the Healthy Acadia Board of Directors. Healthy Acadia is a nonprofit community health organization serving primarily Hancock and Washington counties, in addition to partnering with others to deliver services across the state. We submit this testimony in strong support of LD 1120 and LD 1299.
We support a public health approach to gun safety, to uphold Maine's traditions of safe and appropriate gun use, while supporting common-sense policies regarding access to guns that support the safety and well-being of all Mainers. We believe these measures discussed today meet this goal.
LD 1120, An Act to Promote the Secure Storage of Firearms, promotes common-sense policy, making it a definitive responsibility to safely store a firearm if it may be accessed by a minor or prohibited person. The law requires notice be made by firearm dealers reminding purchasers of this responsibility.
As we've testified in prior hearings, suicide by firearm is a major public health issue for our youth. Safe storage laws help prevent suicide by keeping guns out of the hands of youth and reducing access for lawful adult owners in crisis. Keeping firearms safely stored is a commonsense responsibility to place on gun owners, and no doubt would contribute to reducing accidents and deterring theft.
LD 1299, An Act to Prohibit the Unsecured Storage of Handguns in Motor Vehicles, is another commonsense proposal that will benefit public health. On average, at least one gun is stolen from a car every nine minutes in the United States. Research shows that storing firearms in vehicles

significantly increases the risk of theft, and that the rate of gun thefts from cars tripled from 2013-2023. From 2016-2019, Maine averaged 897 thefts from motor vehicles per year, which rose to 1,450 per year from 2020 to 2023. Requiring having a handgun stored in an unoccupied vehicle to be secured out of sight is a commonsense responsibility for handgun owners. Vehicles thefts make up more than half of gun thefts, often leading to further criminal activity.
Thank you for your time and commitment to a safe community, and I urge you to vote OUGHT to pass on LDs 1120 and 1229.

Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn and distinguished members of the Judiciary

My name is Betsy Williams, I live in Brunswick, and I am speaking today in
opposition to LD 208, An Act to Eliminate the 72-hour Waiting Period on Firearms Purchases and LD 1062, An Act Eliminate Background Checks for Private Sales of
Firearms.
As a member of the Maine State Unitarian Universalist Advocacy Network, I
always look at public policy through the lens of my values and principles.
Over the years, policy debates about guns have leaned heavily on principles of
fairness--fairness to individuals who are responsible gun owners, and individual rights---the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms. These principles---
fairness and citizens' rights----are foundational to our democracy and essential to
hold up when laws are enacted.
The debate about gun safety, however, misses the mark if it considers only these
principles. At the center of the gun safety debate are the moral principles---- foundational to world religions as well as democracy--of compassion, love of
neighbor, and pursuit of the common good. The essential question of the gun safety
debate is: How can we prevent our citizenry from harming themselves and each
other?
These two gun safety bills----along with others you will hear this afternoon----provide
measures of harm prevention: reducing the number of impulsive gun purchases by imposing a modest wait period and requiring background checks on all private gun
sales.
These bills are preventative, not punitive. They respect Maine's long history of responsible gun ownership while confronting the reality that the proliferation of guns, the availability of semi-automatic weapons, and an epidemic of gun violence has changed the calculus for safety regulations.
To borrow a phrase I heard recently "we are living in a moral moment"--in our state and in our nation. Many of the issues of the day ask: are we going to be an amoral society that turns a blind eye to moral principles? Or are We going to be a
strong moral society that supports every effort to do the right thing--which, in the case of gun regulations, includes creating safe conditions for the purchase, use and
storage of firearms.
Please do not turn away from our collective moral responsibility. Vote ONTP on LDs
208 and 1062. Thank you.

Good afternoon Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and members of the Joint Standing Committee On Judiciary. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today on this very significant bill.
My name is Representative Billy Bob Faulkingham, and l serve as the House Republican Leader. I

My name is Madeleine DesFosses, and I am the Advocacy and Public Health Manager for the Maine Chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics (Maine AAP). The Maine AAP is a professional organization of 300 pediatricians and subspecialists who are dedicated to protecting the health of Maine children and adolescents. We are in strong support of LD 1120 and LD 1299, which will help to prevent accidental injuries and deaths, suicide, and gun theft.
In the United States, 4.6 million minors live in homes with at least one loaded, unlocked firearm (2). It only takes a few moments for a curious toddler to open a nightstand drawer and find a gun, or a suicidal teenager to find their parents' firearm tucked away in a closet. In these instances, the safe, secure storage of a firearm can make the difference between injury or death and a narrowly avoided tragedy.
In 2020, a 16-year-old in New Sharon accidentally shot and killed himself after finding a family member's handgun stored in a closet. The next year, a 2-year-old in Waterville was accidentally shot in the head by his sibling with a firearm that was kept in a closet. A few months later, a 2-year-old in West Bath found his parents' unsecured firearm on a nightstand and accidentally shot his parents. Luckily, both parents survived. The common theme is that while all of these incidents were unintentional, they could have been avoided if the firearms used had been stored safely and securely. That's exactly why we need laws that ensure gun owners store their firearms in a safe and secure manner.
Youth suicides can often be prevented through the safe storage of firearms, as the majority (79%) of firearms used in youth suicides belong to a family member of the youth (3). As a resident of Maine for 37 years, a pastor in several Maine churches since 1995, a member of the Maine Council of Churches Public Policy Committee, a former Executive Director of the Maine Council of Churches, and, mostly importantly as a parent and grandparent who has raised children in Maine, I strongly support LD 1120.
From a moral point of view, it strikes me as deeply regrettable that -- knowingly or unconsciously -- we so often apply the "risk-benefit analysis" approach that became prevalent in public policy-making and legal circles over the last 50 or so years to the consideration of policies that touch on matters of human life and death.
In my own Unitarian Universalist and Christian traditions, every other world religion with which I'm familiar, and in humanist philosophy, the idea that every human life is of infinite value is a core belief and central ethical concern. Morally, a human life cannot be put on one side of a scale and money or convenience or traditions on the other.
The value of one human life lost to suicide, accident or violent crime cannot truly be measured. Anyone who hasn't experienced such a loss of a loved one need only ask a grieving family member to see it up close and get a sense of the ripple effects of such tragedies. You have heard testimony today from more than one such grieving person.
The infinite value and worth of every human being is also one of the central ethical principles on which our own Constitution and Bill of Rights rest, although we are still groping our way toward fulfillment of that foundational ideal. We secure self-government and the rights of individuals because the infinite value of human life itself is an intrinsic, or as many people of faith would say, a Divine, truth.
Rather than balancing a proposed policy over against economic effects on small business or big corporations, or the inconvenience to some citizens or the fact that old traditions will need to change in a modern, more interconnected world, we need to put the value of human life at the center and ask whether a particular proposal will detract from or enhance protection of that value. That value will, in some circumstances, demand we put reasonable limits on Constitutional rights that we otherwise hold sacrosanct. Like other Constitutional rights, from a moral point of view (and in line with much legal precedent in many areas of public policy), Second Amendment rights cannot be unbounded and absolute.
In short, gun safety is a public health and safety issue, and a moral issue, not a situation calling for a risk-benefit policy analysis. No amount of economic harm nor the inconvenience of reasonable, common sense limits being placed on a citizen's right to own a dangerous weapon can make up for the infinite loss of the infinite value of a human life that might have been saved.
Proposed public policies such as secure storage of dangerous weapons will self-evidently save human lives. No rational argument could deny this with a straight face. Even if no policy can prevent every tragedy or crime, we have a chance to reduce the likelihood of accidental and suicidal and domestic violence deaths by firearm. Given the infinite value of every human life that would be saved, even if it is only a single one, why would we choose to do any less?
Thank you for considering my views.

Good aftemoon, Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and honorable members of the Joint
Standing Committee on Judiciary. My name is Vicki Doudera and I represent House District 41, Camden and Rockpoit. I am here before you today to present LD 1104, An Act to Limit the Liability of Persons Who Provide Firearm Hold Agreements.
As many of you know, I have been a Maine Realtorm since 2003 and over the course of my
career have had to advise sellers on how best to present their homes to potential buyers. Many
times I have suggested that items be removed from the premises prior to listing, and number one on that list of items are firearms.
A few times this has created a dilemma for the seller who does not have a secure place to store
weapons outside the home. Firearm hold agreements, such as what LD I104 outlines, can solve
this problem. They are designed to provide a safe and temporary solution for managing firearms in a variety of situations: a time when strangers will be touring bedrooms and opening cabinets, such as when a home is listed for sale; a period when inquisitive grandchildren will be visiting from out of state; or a time of upheaval, such as a divorce. All of these are situations when removing firearms from a home might be a good idea.
A year or two ago, I spoke to a gun shop owner in Lewiston who said he wanted to provide this
service for customers but was concerned about his liability. This bill solves that dilemma by providing immunity to the holder of a firearm, in accordance with a firearm hold agreement, who returns the firearm to the owner at the close of the agreed upon loan period.
As written, I believe this bill is too vague and I prefer much of the language in my colleague Representative Wood's version, which you will also hear today. I like that his bill, LD 1174,
specifies that it would be gun shop owners who would be holding the firearms, and I also like the
process outlined for the Department of Public Safety to create the firearm hold agreements.

District 41: Camden and Rockport

However, LD 1174 limits the people who may take advantage of these agreements to veterans
and emergency responders -- probably because these groups are disproportionately affected by the major public health challenge that is firearm suicide. I applaud the sponsor for realizing that firearm hold agreements can perhaps be lifelines for those at risk of harming themselves, but I would argue that allowing the general populace to avail themselves of secure storage is beneficial as well.
In closing, I will repeat what I have often said before this committee when introducing gun
safety legislation: the problem of gun violence in our state is a complex one, requiring creative
solutions on many fronts. Firearm hold agreements are one such solution that can help our fellow
Mainers and hopefully save lives. Thank you for your time and consideration.
